answer: Darshan is a reciprocal looking: the devotee goes to see the deity, but more importantly the deity sees and blesses the devotee. Power runs from the image to the viewer rather than from the viewer who possesses the image (unlike the western voyeuristic gaze). The image looks back and grants something. The author borrows the idea (via Diana Eck and Ravi Vasudevan) as a helpful frame for frontal, iconic address in Hindi film posters and stills, but she hedges. She does not claim every cinematic look is religious darshan or that audiences literally worship stars. She treats it as a suggestive structure of frontality and exchange, not a universal law. [unsure]

The Direct principle is scaled to the objective. For awareness, the ask is soft or absent: the aim is memorability and branding, so no hard call to action is needed. For consideration, the ask gets moderate: invite people to learn more, visit or search. For action/conversion (and for lead or sales objectives), the ask is explicit and repeated: a clear, specific call to action, often supported by on-screen text, voiceover and a CTA end card or overlay, sometimes shown early and again at the end. So directness increases from awareness to consideration to action rather than being one fixed rule. [unsure]

In the glassware chapter, highlights on glass define its surface and shape. A small, bright highlight (from a small source) reads as crisp and sparkling, signalling a hard, polished surface and adding brilliance, but it describes little of the form. A large, dimmer highlight (from a big source such as a large softbox or white card) describes the curvature and the extent of the surface, telling the viewer about shape and volume, while looking softer. What sets the difference in practice is the size of the light source and its distance, relative to the object: the reflection is essentially an image of the source, so source size and brightness determine highlight size and intensity. [unsure]

The Law of Expansion says the power of a brand is inversely proportional to its scope. The obvious objection is giants like GE, Mitsubishi, Yamaha or Samsung that put one name on everything. The authors reply that these firms succeed despite, not because of, line extension: their profit margins and returns are poor compared with focused competitors, and they win in markets lacking strong specialist brands (for example Asia). The cost is that the law becomes hard to falsify: success by a broad brand is redescribed as underperformance relative to a hypothetical focused alternative, or attributed to weak competition, so any counterexample is absorbed and the law's predictive content shrinks. [unsure]

Samara distinguishes a sequential (linear, cinematic) narrative, where the layout unfolds page by page like a story with a beginning, middle and end and elements recur and progress, from a non-sequential or thematic narrative, where spreads are related by concept or variation rather than strict order. When a pictorial, image-driven layout runs over many pages, he claims what stays constant is the underlying structural logic: consistent proportional relationships, recurring alignments and a consistent visual vocabulary (typographic treatment, margins, rhythm), so that even as pictures change dramatically the reader perceives a unified system. [unsure]

Hopkins says keep running the proven campaign in most of the field and test the new approach in a limited portion (a few towns or a fraction of the space) using keyed returns, so the established method continues earning while the challenger is measured against it. He adds that most new schemes fail, suggesting something like three out of four ventures prove wrong, hence the caution. The problem with the 75 per cent figure is that it is an unsupported rule-of-thumb assertion: he gives no data, sample or definition behind it, and it sits awkwardly in a book whose whole argument is that claims should rest on traced, measured results. [unsure]

Godin's two constraints: people share things when sharing it makes them look good or advances their own status/goals (it helps the sharer), and when the thing works better the more people use it (network effects: sharing makes it more valuable to the sharer). Remarkability alone is not enough; the idea must spread because it benefits the person who spreads it. This rules out most attempted 'viral' content, because typical brand assets are made to benefit the marketer: asking people to share an ad gives the sharer nothing, costs them social capital, and the asset gains nothing from being used by more people. [unsure]

Godin's mechanism is that choosing the smallest viable audience lets you understand their worldview, dreams and fears precisely, so you can make something specifically for them that they will find remarkable. Serving 'everyone' forces the work toward the average and bland; serving a specific group lets you make a change they care about, and the work becomes more generous and more useful. Those people then talk about it to others like them, so it spreads horizontally. The improvement comes from empathy and specificity, making the work matter to someone, not from lower reach cost.

The Understanding document starts from 3:1, the minimum contrast recommended by ISO-9241-3 / ANSI-HFES-100-1988 for observers with normal (20/20) vision. It then compensates for contrast sensitivity loss typical of vision around 20/40 (roughly age 80) by a factor of about 1.5, giving 4.5:1. For 7:1 it compensates for loss typical of about 20/80 vision, a factor of about 2.33 (3 x 2.33 = 7). The chain implies the ratios are not perceptual measures of legibility directly; they are the normal-vision baseline scaled by assumed contrast-sensitivity losses for low-vision users, i.e. a proxy for readability by people with reduced vision rather than an intrinsic property of the colours.

Stage one is cultural: in Indian visual culture the frontal face derives from devotional imagery and darshan, where the face/eyes establish contact and exchange between viewer and icon, and the star is displayed like a deity. Stage two is commercial and perceptual: the star's face is the key selling point and the most instantly recognisable element, so leading with it identifies the film and draws the audience. The second stage, the star face as a marketing and recognition device, survives outside the culture (Hollywood posters also sell stars' faces); the darshan-based reading does not transfer. [unsure]

The rule says that in a critique everyone's feedback is equal in the sense that all participants can contribute and ideas are judged on their merit against the objectives, not dismissed because of who offers them; rank should not suppress or inflate comments during the discussion. It is not a claim that decision authority is flattened. It explicitly permits hierarchy to operate in decision-making: after critique, the person responsible (product owner, lead, stakeholder) still makes the call, and seniority or ownership can decide when a decision must be made. Critique is analysis, not decision. [unsure]

An original release poster must introduce an unknown film: announce the stars, genre and story. A re-release poster sells a film the audience already knows (e.g. Mother India, Andaz), often years later to a changed market, so the task is to re-market a classic to new tastes and new generations while appealing to memory and nostalgia. As a result, the designs were updated: newer artistic styles and typography, emphasis shifted toward the most bankable or iconic stars and famous scenes, sometimes foregrounding stars who had become bigger since, and more contemporary colour and composition rather than repeating the original artwork. [unsure]

Under the Law of Quality, the authors say quality perception is built by (1) narrowing the focus: a specialist is perceived as better than a generalist; (2) having a better name; and (3) a high price, since people expect expensive things to be better (Rolex, Mercedes). On price, they argue price is a brand decision made early and deliberately, not derived afterwards from costs: decide to be the high-priced brand in the category as part of the positioning, because price signals quality, and a premium price is a benefit for customers who want to display wealth or quality. [unsure]

Samara describes creating ordered ambiguity through layered transparency and overlapping planes whose structures are related: layers carrying different grids or axes that interpenetrate, so the eye reads alternating foreground and background (figure-ground reversal) while alignments across layers tie them together. He says the effect is strengthened when elements on different layers share alignments or edges, or echo each other in scale, shape or orientation, so that there are clear points of correspondence across the depth, giving the ambiguity a governing logic rather than randomness. [unsure]

Hopkins argues that a named person makes advertising personal: people deal with individuals, not faceless companies, and a man with a name seems to stand behind the product and pledge his reputation, which builds confidence and distinctiveness. Uses he reports include a named doctor or scientist for products (e.g. Dr. Shoop's remedies), named makers or chemists for foods and goods, and personal signatures on offers and letters. He is frank that such names are sometimes invented or chosen for effect: the personality is a device the advertiser creates, rather than always a real originator. [unsure]

Because a photograph is always a slice cut from a continuous visual field, its frame is arbitrary: the photographer could have framed it differently, and anything can be separated, cropped or juxtaposed with anything else. The world becomes a series of unrelated, free-floating fragments, and the edges of the picture do not correspond to natural boundaries of events. A photograph therefore invites deduction, speculation and fantasy: it says 'there is the surface, now think or intuit what is beyond it', but it cannot itself explain or provide understanding, which requires narrative across time.

Boxes show shape through different tonal values on their separate planes; a cylinder has a continuously curving surface, so it needs tonal gradation across its width (a gradient from light to dark) to read as round. Evenly lit, the gradient disappears and it looks flat. The remedy is to light from one side or place a large source/reflector so highlights run along one side and the surface falls off toward the other, or to add a highlight stripe and dark edges. The cost is that part of the can, including label information, falls into darker tone and the label becomes less evenly legible; the highlight also can obscure print. [unsure]

Judged by ABCD: Attract is weak because it lacks fast pacing and tight framing and has no audio hook in a silent open, and it shows no people, missing the human-presence guidance. Brand is wrong: the logo appears only at the end; the source advises branding early (within the first five seconds) and often, visually and in audio. Connect suffers from no people or emotion. What is not wrong: opening on the product is actually encouraged (showing the product early). And the 'Buy now' end card is not strictly an error, but for an awareness objective the Direct principle is relaxed; a hard CTA is unnecessary, though not forbidden. [unsure]

Pandey argues for a network of offices each with genuine local creative leadership and autonomy, rather than a hub-and-spoke model where Mumbai or Delhi creates and branches just service or adapt. Ogilvy India's regional offices (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bangalore, Chennai) should each be creative centres rooted in their local culture and language, sharing one agency culture. The interesting part is the claim that India's diversity means the best national work comes from local insight, so the national agency is stronger as a federation of local creative hubs, and that ideas can travel from the regions to the nation. [unsure]

Brands are brands, companies are companies: customers buy brands, not companies, so marketing should put the brand first and the company name should not dominate. Yet if the company has one dominant brand, making the company name and brand name the same (Coca-Cola, Intel, Xerox) is simplest and strongest. The two sit together because the ideal is a company whose name is its focused brand; problems arise only when a company name is splashed across many brands. The test: is the company name the brand the customer asks for? And does using the company name help or confuse the brand? If the brand is strong, keep the company name subordinate or omit it. [unsure]

The rule: avoid trends; design for longevity, a logo should be timeless and still appropriate decades later. It replaces the standard of being fashionable or current (looking up-to-date now). The concession: identities can be refreshed or evolved over time, and certain trendy treatments in applications can be tolerated, as long as the core mark stays timeless; evolution is acceptable. The problem the rule cannot solve is that no one can know in advance what will look dated: every style is of its time, so 'timeless' can only be judged in hindsight, and even classic marks eventually get redesigned. [unsure]

The loop: when feedback is received poorly or goes nowhere, people stop giving it, so the team gets less and worse feedback, work quality falls, and the culture drifts further from critique. Triggers: (1) the recipient reacts defensively or with hostility, arguing, dismissing, getting upset, so givers feel punished for honesty; (2) feedback is requested but then ignored or not acted upon (no visible effect, no follow-up), so givers conclude it is pointless. Both teach the team that giving feedback is costly or futile, and the supply dries up. [unsure]

No. The source presents the ABCDs as a framework of creative guidelines derived from research into what features correlate with performance (short-term sales likelihood and long-term brand contribution). They help execute and optimise an idea: how to attract attention, brand, connect and direct. They are not a method for generating the core creative idea, and Google notes they complement rather than replace creativity; strong ideas still come from creative talent, and the principles are meant to be applied flexibly, not as a formula. [unsure]

For Hopkins the leverage is in the headline and the appeal (the offer/approach), not the body copy. Changing a headline, he says, can alter returns enormously: he reports differences of several times, even 5x to 10x or more in keyed returns, from the same ad with different headlines. The body copy matters less once the right people are attracted. What he does not supply is a method for finding the winning headline in advance or controlled evidence: the magnitudes are anecdotal reports from keyed tests, without data tables, and he gives no general rule predicting which headline will win; only testing reveals it. [unsure]

Hopkins notes that people judge you by appearances: a salesman in a shabby suit, or a letter on cheap paper, creates distrust, while fine stationery signals quality and conveys prestige. He extends this to advertising: the dress of an ad should suit the product; a cheap-looking ad for a quality product harms it. But he limits the claim: good appearance is not a substitute for salesmanship; he warns against fine writing and artistic effects that are merely decorative. [unsure]

Jain argues calendar catalogues (from printing presses in Sivakasi etc.) reflect a chain of intermediaries, not consumer desire directly. Layers: artists produce images to suit publishers' briefs and past sellers; publishers select what to print based on what distributors and agents order; agents and wholesalers order what they think retailers and commercial clients (businesses giving calendars as gifts) will take; the buyers are often firms whose calendars are giveaways, so the image choice reflects the patron's promotional needs. The end user often does not choose. Therefore catalogues record producers' and intermediaries' expectations, conventions and risk-aversion, shaped by existing successes, not a transparent index of consumer preference. [unsure]

SC 1.4.8 Visual Presentation (Level AAA) requires that a mechanism or presentation supports line spacing (leading) of at least space-and-a-half within paragraphs, plus paragraph spacing larger, among other things (width, justification, colours). It concerns how text is presented, or that users can select it. SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing (AA) does not require the content to be presented that way; it requires that when users override styles to line height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2x, letter spacing 0.12x and word spacing 0.16x font size, no content or functionality is lost. Satisfy 1.4.8 by default presentation or a user control; satisfy 1.4.12 by layouts that tolerate user-applied spacing without clipping or overlap.

After listing the qualities of an iconic logo (simple, relevant, enduring, distinctive, memorable, small-scale, focused on one thing), Airey says these are not unbreakable rules: designers can break them. The precondition is that you must first know and understand the rules well before breaking them deliberately. The benefit claimed is that breaking them knowingly can produce something more distinctive and memorable, standing out from the conventional. [unsure]

The rule: do not rely on opinion or guesswork; test everything and let the public decide through traced returns, because the advertiser's judgment is usually wrong. His concession: he himself, even after long experience, is often wrong in guessing what will work; his instinct fails, so he tests. He offers a ratio such as being right perhaps only a minority of times, or new ventures failing in most cases. What is wrong with the ratio is that it is an unmeasured, anecdotal estimate: the author who insists on data offers a figure with no count or record behind it, so it is itself an untested guess. [unsure]

Desai's Imperfect Solution thesis: Indian consumers often prefer a good-enough, affordable, adaptable product over a perfect expensive one; jugaad-like tolerance of imperfection, where what matters is fit to constraints. The general part: products designed for resource-constrained users should prioritise affordability and adaptability over completeness; that has force across markets. The parts that are asserted as uniquely Indian cultural character (a national temperament) have no general force and are anecdotal. The separation matters because a brand should adopt the design principle (affordability-led, flexible) based on constraint economics, not on cultural stereotypes that may not hold across segments or over time. [unsure]

Samara treats repeating the label elsewhere as a crutch that undermines the composition's integrity: it adds redundancy and breaks the visual logic without solving the hierarchy problem. He prefers fixing the relationships within the dense field: adjusting contrast, scale, weight or colour of the label, or shifting and clearing surrounding elements, so the information emerges from the texture while remaining integrated. [unsure]

Sontag says people want the idealised image: to look their best, to be beautified, rather than to be shown truthfully. The news that the camera could lie made being photographed more popular. The inference rule: when a portrait is flattering, people take it as truthful; photography's value is in its claim to fidelity, but in practice people want a photograph that looks good and still accept it as evidence, so a photograph that shows them unflatteringly is deemed a bad photograph. [unsure]

Desai argues the Indian household runs on value-seeking in everyday consumption so that surplus can be saved and deployed for socially significant occasions. Thrift and extravagance serve the same logic: family status, obligations and social capital. Everyday frugality is a means; the wedding is an investment in family honour, networks and marriage prospects, a once-in-a-lifetime ritual expenditure that the whole community evaluates. So spending on the wedding is the goal that the frugality was saving for, not an inconsistency. [unsure]

The observation: Indian consumers historically did not prioritise safety features (e.g. car airbags, helmets), and safety-led messaging rarely sold. The explanation offered is cultural: fatalism or a belief that fate, God or providence protects, and a tendency to value the family's immediate needs over hypothetical risk. The observation carries more weight since it reflects market behaviour; the cultural explanation is speculative and anecdotal, alternative explanations like price sensitivity and lack of regulation exist. A brand leading on safety should not assume it is futile, but should test. [unsure]

They say 'feedback' in its original sense comes from systems/engineering (cybernetics, electrical circuits): output fed back into a system as input, a signal of how the system responded. So feedback denotes any reaction, including gut reactions, not necessarily useful analysis. Asking for 'feedback' therefore invites any response: likes and dislikes, direction, or reactions. It follows that you must be specific about the kind of feedback wanted, distinguishing critique (analysis against objectives) from reaction and direction, and framing requests to get critique. [unsure]

Berger has students in class rate or choose something, e.g. the size of a candy/food/intended donation or choosing among options, where some see others' choices. He describes his class exercise: students guess the length of a line or similar, after hearing others' answers. The result: students' answers converge toward what others said (conformity, similar to Asch). He concedes an alternative explanation: that people may be using others' answers as informative (information rather than normative pressure), or that students might simply rely on the answers because they lack knowledge. [unsure]

Samara says a centred, symmetrical layout relies on the wide field around the central axis to create a sense of stasis, formality and breathing space; on a narrow phone screen the margins collapse and everything stacks in a single column, so the tension between content and space, and the hierarchy of scale, is lost. To recover some of it, he suggests adjusting proportions and spacing in the responsive grid: preserving generous vertical intervals, contrast in scale and type size, and inset margins so the centred axis still reads, i.e. translating horizontal space into vertical rhythm. [unsure]

Bijapurkar's claim is that Indian demand is pyramid-shaped: most households are at the bottom and middle, and the numbers of consumers are large but per-capita consumption is small; aggregate demand is dominated by the large base of lower-income households. The worked case: a product category where the top 'rich' segment has high penetration but small absolute numbers; the bulk of volume actually comes from the middle/lower segments, so growth depends on the 'consuming class' not the elite. So the segment that matters for market size is the large, lower-income mass, not the premium top. [unsure]

The variable is viewing time and context: a roadside board is seen at speed for a couple of seconds, while a subway poster is seen by a captive audience waiting on a platform. For the roadside board, Sullivan permits only a very short line, one image, one idea, seven words or fewer; for the subway poster, longer copy and more complex, even funny ideas can work because people have time to read. Tests: can it be understood at a glance (the drive-by test), and is it simple enough, i.e., does the one thing still read when looked at quickly from a distance. [unsure]

Jain describes a nationalist injunction favouring muscular Hindu masculinity; the breach is that in calendar art, images of gods like Ram and Krishna became softer and more androgynous in the late twentieth century, while at the same time other trends (e.g. the muscular Ram of the 1980s-90s Hindutva era) emerged. She accepts from Patricia Uberoi (or Anuradha Kapur) the observation of the shift from gentle to militant iconography, but departs by arguing it is not a simple progression; the soft, eroticised body persists alongside, and she reads it through bazaar corporeality rather than purely political ideology. [unsure]

In the reproduced National Dairy Development Board Operation Flood frames, the word 'doodh' appears prominently in the frame, in Devanagari, integrated with the image, often as a single dominant word rather than in a body of copy. That placement buys instant recognition across literacy levels and languages: a single familiar word acts as a label, anchoring the image's meaning and making milk the subject even for barely literate audiences, while giving a national, Hindi-inflected identity. [unsure]

Ogilvy advises against double-page spreads because they rarely get proportionally higher readership than single pages, so they are bad value. In a footnote he corrects that a spread gets about a third more readership, which is not worth double the cost, but can be worth it in specific cases, e.g. when you need the space for a long list of facts or a big demonstration, or to impress the trade. The corrected version is more useful because it replaces a blanket prohibition with a cost-per-reader calculation you can apply case by case. [unsure]

The book frames the choice between rules and standards along two factors: the costs of decisions (effort of case-by-case judgment) and the costs of errors (noise and bias from discretion). A vague standard invites level and pattern noise but adapts to cases; a list of disqualifying conditions reduces noise and decision costs but may be over- and under-inclusive and invite gaming. If errors from noise are costly and cases fairly uniform, rules win. Afterwards, it says to monitor for the rules producing bad outcomes, i.e. whether errors arise from rigidity or from people circumventing rules (gaming), and adjust. [unsure]

In ordinary usage 'iconic' means famous, emblematic. Kapur's iconicity refers to a specific mode of representation from Indian devotional art: frontal, static, symmetrical presentation of a figure addressed directly to the viewer, with symbolic attributes, flatness and a hieratic quality, rather than narrative, perspectival realism. It matters because it shifts reading from 'what story is happening' to a mode of address: images are to be looked at and to look back (darshan), meaning lies in the figure's presence and attributes, not in a depicted moment. [unsure]

Ogilvy says business-to-business ads work by the same principles as consumer ads: use headlines that promise a benefit, give facts and specifics, use long copy since technical buyers read, use testimonials and case histories, demonstrations, and news. The proposed ad is a style-over-substance, with lifestyle imagery irrelevant to valves and too few words. Ogilvy would add product specifications, case histories, a benefit headline, and a mechanism for measuring: a coupon/reply mechanism or offer (a free booklet, technical literature) so inquiries can be counted, plus readership (Starch) scores. [unsure]

This is Robert Cialdini's Petrified Forest study. The sign describing that many past visitors had taken wood ('Many past visitors have removed petrified wood...') actually increased theft, nearly tripling it compared with the other sign, which asked visitors not to remove wood to preserve the park and reduced theft. The general rule: descriptive social norms backfire when you publicise that an undesired behaviour is common; making a behaviour public makes it seem normal and can encourage it. Do not tell people that lots of others are doing the thing you want to stop.

Sontag says photographs may be more memorable than moving images because they are neat slices of time, not a flow: a still can be kept, revisited and becomes a memory marker. Television and film are streams of images, each cancelling its predecessor, and film controls the viewer's time and attention, taking away the viewer's freedom to linger; the pace is set for you. The cost of stasis: a photograph cannot explain; it lacks narrative, it can only show a moment without context, so understanding, which works through time, is impossible from the still alone; it fragments. [unsure]

Godin says 'better' is relative to what a particular audience values: every product sits on axes the person cares about (price, speed, convenience, status, etc.), and better for one person is worse for another. Since preferences differ, there is no single ranking, so 'better' is not transitive across people; you can only be better for someone. He exempts some things: objective measures like performance specs or safety still exist, but they matter only if people care; perhaps ethical elements, i.e. not being a scam. [unsure]

Bijapurkar reverses the usual question 'Is India a market for my product?' or 'How big is the market for my product?' to 'What is the Indian market, and what product/business model fits it?' Instead of starting from the product and looking for Indian consumers who look like the company's existing customers, the analyst first studies Indian consumers: their incomes, structure, behaviour and where the demand is, and then designs offerings and price points for that demand. It changes the first step from product-led market sizing to consumer-led market understanding. [unsure]

Carroll's mechanism is that shallow depth of field blurs out the background and foreground, removing distracting detail so that the only sharp thing left is the subject. The subject stands out because everything else is subtracted, not because the subject is given more sharpness or emphasis. The distinction matters because it tells you that the technique is about reducing clutter: if the background is already simple, shallow focus adds little, and you can achieve the same isolation by other subtractive means (clean backgrounds, framing), rather than relying on lens settings. [unsure]

Sullivan says people fire back 'So what?' and 'Who cares?' ... pairing them: to 'So what?' respond with a benefit, why it matters to them; to 'Prove it' / 'Oh yeah?' respond with proof, evidence or demonstration. If you cannot provide proof (the product has no demonstrable superiority), he suggests making the brand likable through the way you say it, using charm, honesty, or humour, i.e. make up in style and tone what you lack in proof. [unsure]

Starbucks is praised for contracting to a narrow focus (premium coffee) and building through publicity rather than advertising. But the book notes, in passing, that Starbucks has expanded into other things: ice cream, bottled drinks, music, and many products with its name, or that it now advertises. This matters because it shows the authors' showcase case may itself violate the law, and the brand kept succeeding while expanding, which weakens the causal claim that contraction produced the success; a reader should see that the case supports correlation at a moment, not the law. [unsure]

The gobo above the subject blocks light to create a dark area/edge definition (e.g. keeping the top of glossy objects dark, or defining edges of glass). It stops working when the subject is too tall, or when the camera view includes the gobo, or when the gobo must be too close and shows in reflections. Instead the book offers using a large light behind with black cards on the sides, or light from below/background, or post-production, or darkening edges using black cards placed beside the subject out of frame. [unsure]

Bijapurkar says her numbers are snapshots that date quickly because India changes fast; readers should treat specific figures as illustrative, focus on the structural patterns and frameworks, and update with current data. The Canon record (the local knowledge base) notes the data vintage, flags numbers as time-bound and not to be used as current fact, and stores the method/pattern rather than the figure, marking them as historical. [unsure]

In the Grand Canyon picture, the landscape becomes flat planes due to: a telephoto lens compressing perspective, atmospheric haze/aerial perspective, and backlighting or low sun toward the camera giving silhouette. The mechanism carries through the lighting and haze: the backlight into haze reduces each ridge to a single tone without detail, with each successive ridge lighter, so the ridges read as flat cut-out layers. The telephoto enables framing but the tonal separation through atmosphere is the key. [unsure]

WCAG success criteria apply to the default presentation provided by the author. SC 1.4.3 notes that if the content is presented by default meeting contrast, and users have a mechanism to choose alternative styles, low contrast chosen by the user is not a failure. The Understanding doc explicitly says users may choose colour combinations with low contrast, and that is acceptable, as long as the default (or a readily available mode) meets the ratio. So a reading mode with low-contrast presets is allowed, provided the default presentation conforms and the user chooses the preset.

Hopkins says to start local and test in a few towns because national magazine advertising is expensive and a mistake is costly; local tests using newspapers let you trace results, learn cost per customer and sales, and discover the right approach cheaply before spending nationally. Once proven, you can extend to magazines. His scope limit: this applies to products which need distribution through local dealers and can be tested locally; for some mail-order or specialty goods (where local testing isn't practical), magazines may be right from the start. [unsure]

Ogilvy reports that in direct mail, letters with more copy often outpull short letters, and that personalising or adding more enclosures increases response. Two counterintuitive results: a long letter outperformed a short one, and a letter with a postscript or an unprepossessing plain envelope outpulled a slick one. These items carry more weight because direct mail is measured precisely by coupon or order returns in split tests, so results are directly observed, unlike his inferences from readership or recall studies. [unsure]

Hopkins: what the maker thinks too ordinary is often the best selling point, because the public does not know it: the first to tell it gets credit for it (Schlitz steam-cleaned bottles, pure water from deep wells). So you should use the ordinary detail. The thing he is proudest of may matter to him but not to customers; it may be uninteresting to buyers or not unique. You should judge by what the consumer would find impressive, not by the maker's pride. [unsure]

The analogy school predicts India's future consumption by comparing it with where other countries (China, South Korea, Southeast Asia) were at similar income levels, assuming India will follow the same path. The objection: India is different, its demand structure, income distribution, culture, and slow growth path mean that analogies mislead; India's consumers behave in their own way, and the country has multiple markets coexisting. Using analogies leads to wrong forecasts and to strategies designed for another country. [unsure]

Raking light shows texture by creating tiny highlights and shadows on the surface. For the light sponge, the diffuse surface reflects so highlights and shadows contrast. For black leather, the surface is dark with low diffuse reflection and is somewhat glossy: the texture is visible mainly through direct reflections; raking light from the side produces little diffuse contrast and its direct reflections go away from the camera, so the texture disappears. The remedy: light from a position that produces direct reflection (within the family of angles) using a large, not too diffuse source, so the texture shows as highlights. [unsure]

Hopkins escalated risk transfer from the advertiser: free samples, then money-back guarantees, then letting customers try the product first and pay later, or buying a product at the dealer's risk (e.g. the coupon that pays the dealer for a free package). His general finding: people who are trusted are honest; very few abuse a guarantee or free trial. His counter-case: some offer where people did abuse it or where free sampling was wasteful, e.g. giving to people who would not buy. [unsure]

The book advises not to explain every decision up front: first, explaining everything takes time and leaves less for critique; second, it biases the critics and preempts their fresh reactions, and they will not see the design as a user would. The rule: give just the context necessary: the objectives, the problem, the constraints, and what you want feedback on, and leave other decisions to be discovered and discussed. [unsure]

The book says noise does not cancel out in real systems because each judgment affects a specific person or case: a too-harsh sentence and a too-lenient sentence do not cancel, they are two errors. In mean squared error, bias and noise contribute independently; errors add up as squares. Cancellation only happens when judgments are aggregated, e.g. averaging multiple independent judgments of the same case (the wisdom of crowds), where the average has less noise. Single decisions do not benefit.

The attrition argument: part one, repeated exposure to images of suffering dulls our response; shock fades. Part two, which is the mechanism, is that photographs make events seem real at first, but with repetition they make them less real: the image becomes familiar, a spectacle, and the viewer's capacity for feeling is used up. Her example contrasts the first time she saw Holocaust photographs (Bergen-Belsen, Dachau) at twelve, producing a lasting negative epiphany, with later images of the Vietnam war, which viewers are anaesthetised to. [unsure]

SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast does not apply to logos or brand names that are part of a logo; but a logo loses its exemption when it is used as a control (e.g. a link to the home page) or conveys information as part of UI component. Actually the source says logotypes are exempt, but if graphics in the logo are required to understand content, they need contrast. Worked case: a logo used as a home link where the logo itself is the control indicator must have contrast; or a logo that includes an icon required to understand. [unsure]

'Black magic' is the technique of using black cards or flags (black surfaces) positioned near the subject to create dark reflections on glossy surfaces or dark edges on glass, a subtractive lighting technique. On metal and glass, reflections of black cards produce dark lines that define shape. Its hardness (sharpness of the edge) is controlled by distance: the closer the black card is to the subject, or the further from focus, the softer or sharper the edge; a black card further from the subject gives a harder edge, near gives soft. [unsure]

Bijapurkar's rules: use the NCAER/MISH income survey data for structure not absolute levels; treat household income numbers as underreported; look at distribution shapes and changes over time; use income bands consistently; triangulate with consumption data. She credits the data to NCAER (National Council of Applied Economic Research), notably Rajesh Shukla's work on the Market Information Survey of Households. [unsure]

Two design moves: small unit packs (sachets) that lower the price per purchase, and lower price points or pay-per-use models. The evidence reported includes sales growth and penetration numbers from companies; the part that is not evidence is the anecdote or a company claim of success presented as proof, e.g. the claim that sachets created a market, with no counterfactual. [unsure]

Godin's argument: people do not change their minds because of facts or because you are right; the status quo is maintained by culture, 'people like us do things like this'. Change happens through tension, status and affiliation: marketers create tension that can be relieved by joining the group or shifting status. In Chapter Nine the chain: people like us -> do things like this -> culture defines normal; to shift the status quo you must change what people like us do, starting with early adopters, who influence the next group. [unsure]

The asymmetry: a painting is judged as an object made by an artist; a fake painting lies about authorship, falsifying art history. A photograph is valued as a trace of reality; a fake photograph lies about what existed, falsifying reality. The detail easy to miss: Sontag defines a fake photograph as one that has been retouched or tampered with, or whose caption is false, i.e. a photograph can be 'fake' via caption without the image altered. [unsure]

Itiel Dror's studies showed that fingerprint examiners, told contextual information (e.g. the suspect confessed or had an alibi), changed their conclusions on the same prints they had previously examined. Moreover, the context affected what they perceived: which features they noticed in the prints. This matters because remedies cannot rely on the expert just correcting their conclusion; you must control information flow (linear sequential unmasking), shielding examiners from irrelevant context before they analyse the evidence.

Freeman says a collage coheres when (1) the individual images share a common element or theme (visual consistency, like similar tone, colour, subject or treatment), and (2) there is an overall structure or design, a dominant organising pattern, so the parts relate to each other and the whole reads as one image rather than a list. [unsure]

Ogilvy says testimonials in TV should be from real customers, and they are more credible when the person is not a polished performer: when viewers see a polished speaker they suspect an actor, which destroys belief. He recommends candid-camera or hidden-camera interviews: filming real people unaware, which produces conviction because the audience sees spontaneity. [unsure]

The brief is a vague truism: it states a belief that could apply to anyone and gives no specific insight or tension. It is not a strategic statement that a creative can argue against or build on; it says nothing about the target, the brand, or why it matters. The general diagnosis: briefs that are generic platitudes offer nothing to create against. A good brief should contain a sharp, specific insight or proposition, and one thing to say. [unsure]

Pandey offers: chase awards with scam work, or do real work for real clients that wins in the marketplace. He argues the mechanism is that real work builds a lasting reputation, client trust, and craft; and great real work also wins awards. Asserted without evidence: that good real work will eventually win awards and that scam work harms careers. [unsure]

Objective ignorance is the unpredictability inherent in the world: information that no one could know when making a judgment (future events, chance). Noise is unwanted variability in judgments of the same case, which can be reduced. Even if prediction accuracy is limited by objective ignorance, reducing noise gives small improvements (e.g. correlation gains) that, applied across many decisions, yield meaningful benefits; small increases in accuracy are valuable across large numbers of cases.

Godin says trying to please everyone leads to mediocrity: widening to the mass audience makes the work average because each round of feedback comes from people who aren't the audience and each objection sands off what made it remarkable. The mechanism operates inside the team or organisation: feedback and approvals push toward safe, bland outcomes, before it reaches the market. [unsure]

Ogilvy found drawings do better for some products, e.g. when a photograph would look unappetising or when the subject cannot be photographed well; the case he gives is a Guinness or food ad, or illustrations in ads for Rolls-Royce? The reversal: when the photograph fails to be more realistic or believable. It shows photographs win because they are perceived as real and believable, not because of any intrinsic appeal. [unsure]

The source establishes that star images in Indian film publicity rely on recognisable facial features, frontal address and iconography, and that star identity is central to publicity. It can justify that recognition features (face, style, costume) drive posters. It cannot justify reproducing a real performer's likeness: the source does not address rights, consent, or legitimacy; its historical analysis is descriptive, so any control reproducing a named performer would lack permission basis. [unsure]

Ogilvy would change: reverse type (white on dark) reduces readership, so use black type on white; sans-serif is harder to read, use serif; full-page-width column is too wide, use narrower columns; headline should be below the photograph; add captions because captions are read more than body copy. Reasons: all based on readership research.

The engineering point: a scooter (e.g. Bajaj Chetak) with small wheels and a side-offset engine is less stable than a motorcycle. The perception came from its design, a covered body protecting feet and the family image (family riding), feeling safe. The engineering claim is plausible but not rigorously supported; the perception is argued with anecdote and advertising, so weaker support. [unsure]

The 30% and 17% figures (ads following ABCDs show 30% lift in short-term sales likelihood and 17% lift in long-term brand contribution) come from a Google/Ipsos (with Kantar?) study, 'ABCD MMM analysis' 2022. The Think with Google page gives the sample size (e.g. analysis of thousands of ads). [unsure]

The front face is reflecting the dark surroundings (camera area), because for a metal box the front face mirrors what's in front of it; the bottom edge disappears because it's dark tone against dark surface. The easiest answer: place a large white card or light source in front, reflecting in the front face, and elevate or use a light-toned surface or edge highlight to separate the bottom. [unsure]

The source says audio brand mentions: including brand name in voiceover or sound early leads to higher performance, e.g. ads that mention the brand in the audio and visually outperform. It's an interactive claim: combined audio+visual brand mentions lift performance more than either alone. [unsure]

In the objective table, Direct is left at 'Apply core principles' for awareness, Connect maybe for action... The pattern: the framework emphasises different principles per objective, prioritising what matters most for each goal; so it is not uniform, it's weighted. [unsure]
